paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Vayeira 117a (quotation preserved in Pri Tzaddik). English translation of source: “‘When the letter vav is completed within ten six times, there are sixty [stages] to raise [it] from the dust. At each sixty of that sixth millennium, the heh gains strength and rises through its levels. In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, together with the springs of wisdom below; and the world will be prepared to enter the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, when the sun begins to set, to enter Shabbos. ... Your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the springs of the great deep broke open’ [Genesis 7:11].’” Context and connection: These are the central clauses explicitly transmitted in Rav Tzadok’s text. His explanation identifies the upper opening with the illumination of Written Torah and the lower wellsprings with Oral Torah and inner transformation; the image is interpreted within his account of teshuvah and yesod, not as a claim about any particular technology. The exact Zohar pagination varies by edition.

paragraphs.text: Further parallel — Tiferet Yosef, Noach 1 [paragraph 7] (English translation as supplied in Akiva Publishing interlinear library): “My revered father, my master and teacher, of blessed memory, explained regarding this that the primary beginning of the World of Rectification (Olam HaTikkun) began from Noah onward. For prior to Noah, existence was still within the state of the “worlds that were destroyed” (almin de-itcharavu). And as we see, previously it is written (Genesis 4:1-2): “and she bore Cain... and she bore further his brother Abel” — where there was as yet no cohesion or connection between one and the other; whereas from Noah onward the World of Rectification began, and here it is written: “Shem, Ham, and Japheth” linked together with the connecting 'vav' and direct accusatives, indicating that they possessed mutual connection and integration.”

And...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

paragraphs.text: Kisvei Beis Ishbitz–Radzin Parallel — Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 8: “Now the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field. From this it appears that in the wild beasts of the field is found more wisdom than in domestic animals, for a domestic beast agrees in its mindset to be subjugated and disciplined under the hand of man, with man providing sustenance for its soul, and does not care to sustain its needs directly from Hashem's hand; whereas in the wild beast is found greater wisdom, in that it does not wish to receive its bounty through flesh and blood, and consents to live with measured austerity, provided that its sustenance be directly from Hashem, blessed be He, so that it gazes at all times unto the Giver.” Connection to this note: This Beis Ishbitz–Radzin teaching in Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Genesis, Bereshit 8 clarifies the inner dimension of Zohar, Vayechi 23:182-26:195 and directly illuminates Rav Tzadok's point in Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom.

paragraphs.text: Shabbat 146a: ‘the snake came upon Eve, i.e., when it seduced her to eat from the Tree of Knowledge, it infected her with moral contamination, and this contamination remained in all human beings. When the Jewish people stood at Mount Sinai, their contamination ceased, whereas gentiles did not stand at Mount Sinai, and their contamination never ceased. Rav Aḥa, the son of Rava, said to Rav Ashi: What about converts? How do you explain the cessation of their moral contamination? Rav Ashi said to him: Even though they themselves were not at Mount Sinai, their guardian angels were present, as it is written: “It is not with you alone that I make this covenant and this oath, but with he that stands here with…’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Shabbat 146a) to illuminate his statement here (“(as written in Shabbat 146a), and from this the contamination adhered to Adam the First as well, and through this he became stretched in his foreskin (as stated in Sanhedrin 38b), meaning that he was certainly...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 38b: ‘Rav Yehuda says that Rav says: Adam the first man spanned from one end of the world until the other, as it is stated: “Since the day that God created man upon the earth, and from the one end of heaven unto the other” (Deuteronomy 4:32), meaning that on the day Adam was created he spanned from one end of the heavens until the other. Once Adam sinned, the Holy One, Blessed be He, placed His hand on him and diminished him, as it is stated: “Behind and before You have created me and laid Your hand upon me” (Psalms 139:5), that at first Adam spanned “behind and before,” meaning everywhere, and then God laid His hand on him and diminished him.’ Context and connection to Pri Tzaddik: In Peri Tzadik, Noach 6 — The Sixth Millennium and the Gates of Wisdom, Rav Tzadok cites this talmudic and halakhic source (Sanhedrin 38b) to illuminate his statement here (“(as stated in Sanhedrin 38b), meaning that he was certainly created circumcised, and through the corruption he became stretched in his foreskin; and since this occurred on the sixth day within the days of Creation,...”), showing how the inner meaning of the source grounds the spiritual dynamic of Torah, divine service, and the rectification of the heart developed in this discourse of Pri Tzaddik.

paragraphs.text: Sanhedrin 97a. English translation of source: “‘Rav Ketina said: The world lasts six thousand years, and for one [thousand years] it is desolate, as it says, ‘And the Lord alone shall be exalted on that day’ [Isaiah 2:11]. Abaye said: For two [thousand years] it is desolate, as it says, ‘After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, and we shall live before Him’ [Hosea 6:2].’” Context and connection: Rav Tzadok cites the seven-thousand-year pattern and relates it to the six days of creation followed by Shabbos. His further division of the millennia according to divine attributes supplies the conceptual bridge to Noach’s six-hundredth year. The passage should be read as theological symbolism within the rabbinic discussion, not as an independently verified prediction.

paragraphs.text: Isaiah 3:10; Chagigah 12a. English translation of source: “Isaiah 3:10: ‘Say of the righteous that it shall be good, for they will eat the fruit of their deeds.’ Chagigah 12a: ‘Rabbi Elazar said: By the light that the Holy One, blessed be He, created on the first day, Adam could look from one end of the world to the other. When the Holy One saw the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion, and saw that their deeds were corrupt, He arose and concealed it from them, as it says, ‘Their light is withheld from the wicked’ [Job 38:15]. paragraphs.text: Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 16; Genesis 11:1. English translation of source: “‘Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: They instituted the joining of courtyards [eiruvei chatzeiros] only for the sake of peace. How so? The Holy One, blessed be He, said: ‘I make peace in My world, but these wicked ones are setting out to bring strife into the world.’ How do we know that they disputed with the Holy One? His parallel is that some forms of spiritual damage require Torah’s transformative wisdom rather than merely the familiar modes of repentance.

paragraphs.text: Zohar I, Vayeira 117a (conclusion as preserved in Pri Tzaddik). English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, and the springs of wisdom below, and the world will be readied to enter into the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, once the sun has begun to set, to enter into Shabbos. So too [with the world]. And your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the fountains of the great deep burst open’ [Genesis 7:11].’” Context and connection: The sequence of images is essential: opening wisdom is preparation for a sanctified seventh period, not an end in itself. Rav Tzadok interprets the number six hundred through the six middos and the human task of refining desire; the final approach to Shabbos denotes a divine completion beyond human effort. English translation of source: “‘In the six-hundredth year of the sixth [millennium], the gates of wisdom above will open, and the springs of wisdom below, and the world will be readied to enter into the seventh, like a person preparing on the sixth day, once the sun has begun to set, to enter into Shabbos. So too [with the world]. And your sign is: ‘In the six-hundredth year of Noah’s life ... all the fountains of the great deep burst open’ [Genesis 7:11].’” Context and connection: The sequence of images is essential: opening wisdom is preparation for a sanctified seventh period, not an end in itself. Rav Tzadok interprets the number six hundred through the six middos and the human task of refining desire; the final approach to Shabbos denotes a divine completion beyond human effort. The wording follows the excerpt in Pri Tzaddik because Zohar editions use differing foliation.
